hello.title: Hello, assembly
hello.summary: Write your first assembly program and print text with the write and exit system calls.
hello.lesson.0: A processor (CPU) does not understand Python or Go. It runs **machine code**: numbers that stand for very small steps, like "copy this number" or "add these two numbers". **Assembly language** gives each step a short name, such as `mov` or `add`. A program called an **assembler** turns your assembly text into machine code. In this course you write assembly for x86-64 processors on Linux, with the assembler NASM.
hello.lesson.2: The first line, `default rel`, is a setting for NASM: it tells NASM how to find the data. Write it at the top of every program. After it, a program has **sections**: `section .data` holds data and `section .text` holds the instructions. The line `msg db "Hello, world!", 10` puts bytes into memory. `msg` is a **label**: a name for the place where the bytes start. `db` (define bytes) stores the characters of the text, and `10` is the newline character that ends the line.
hello.lesson.4: `_start:` is a label for the first instruction. A label in the code ends with a colon `:`. Linux starts your program at `_start`. The line `global _start` makes this name visible to the **linker**, the tool that turns the assembled code into a program you can run.
hello.lesson.5: Each line after `_start:` is one **instruction**. `mov rax, 1` copies the number `1` into `rax`. The names `rax`, `rdi`, `rsi` and `rdx` are **registers**: small, fast storage places inside the CPU. The next unit explains them.
hello.lesson.7: Your program cannot print by itself. It asks Linux to do it with a **system call**. You put the number of the system call into `rax` and its inputs into `rdi`, `rsi` and `rdx`. Then the instruction `syscall` hands the work to Linux.
hello.lesson.8: System call `1` is **write**. `rdi` says where to write: `1` is the screen (standard output). `rsi` is the address of the first byte, here `msg`. `rdx` is the number of bytes: `Hello, world!` has 13 characters, plus 1 for the newline, so `14`. System call `60` is **exit**: it ends the program, and `rdi` holds the exit code. `0` means that everything went well.
hello.lesson.10: The first write prints only 5 bytes, so you see `Hello` without a newline, and `Bye` follows on the same line. `syscall` puts its result into `rax` (for write, the number of bytes written). That is why you set `rax` again before the next system call.
hello.lesson.11: Never forget the exit call. Without it, the CPU continues with whatever bytes come after your last instruction, and the program crashes with a **segmentation fault**.
hello.lesson.12: Text after a semicolon `;` is a comment, and NASM ignores it. Empty lines and the spaces at the start of a line only make the code easier to read.
hello.card.0: `default rel` first, then `section .data` for data and `section .text` for code
hello.card.1: `global _start` and `_start:` mark where the program begins
hello-1.options.0: It turns assembly text into machine code
hello-1.options.2: It prints text on the screen
hello-1.explain: An assembler such as NASM translates the instructions you write into the numbers the CPU runs. Linux starts the finished program.
hello-2.explain: `rdx` is `4`, so the write call prints only the first 4 bytes of the text.
hello-3.statement: Linux starts a program at the first line of `section .data`.
hello-3.explain: Linux starts at the label `_start`. `section .data` holds data, not instructions.
hello-4.prompt: Which value in `rax` selects the system call exit?
hello-4.explain: Exit is system call `60`. Write is system call `1`.
hello-5.prompt: Complete the code so it prints Hi.
hello-5.explain: System call `1` is write. `60` would end the program, and `msg` is an address, not a system call number.
hello-6.prompt: How many bytes must `rdx` hold to print this whole line, including the newline?
hello-6.explain: `Assembly is fun` has 15 characters (the spaces count too), and the newline `10` is one more byte.
hello-7.prompt: Build the line that selects the system call exit.
hello-7.explain: The system call number goes into `rax`, and exit is `60`. The destination comes first.
hello-8.prompt: Build the data line that stores Hi followed by a newline.
hello-8.explain: `db` stores bytes, and the newline is the number `10` after a comma. NASM does not turn `\n` in double quotes into a newline.
hello-9.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
hello-9.pairs.2: asks Linux to do the work
hello-9.pairs.4: the place where the program starts
hello-10.prompt: These lines should print Hi. Which line has the bug?
hello-10.explain: `60` is the system call exit, so the program ends without printing. Write `mov rax, 1`.
hello-11.prompt: These lines should print OK. Which line has the bug?
hello-11.explain: Text needs quotes. Without them, NASM looks for a label called `OK`. Write `msg db "OK", 10`.
hello-12.statement: After `syscall`, `rax` still holds the number of the system call.
hello-12.explain: `syscall` puts its result into `rax`. After a write, `rax` holds the number of bytes written, so you set `rax` again before the next system call.
registers.title: Registers and mov
registers.summary: Store numbers and characters in registers, copy them with mov and use the smaller parts of a register.
registers.lesson.0: A **register** is a small storage place inside the CPU. The CPU works with registers much faster than with memory. An x86-64 CPU has 16 general-purpose registers, and each one holds 64 bits (8 bytes).
registers.lesson.1: Their names are `rax`, `rbx`, `rcx`, `rdx`, `rsi`, `rdi`, `rbp`, `rsp` and `r8` to `r15`. You can use most of them for your own values. `rsp` is special: it always points to the stack (unit 7), so do not use it for other values.
registers.lesson.3: `mov destination, source` copies the source into the destination. The destination comes first. The source can be a number written in the code (an **immediate**) or another register. The source keeps its value.
registers.lesson.5: `mov rbx, 5` puts `5` into `rbx`. `mov rdx, rbx` copies it into `rdx`, so the write call prints 5 bytes. After the copy, both registers hold `5`.
registers.lesson.7: You can also use parts of a register. `eax` is the lower 32 bits of `rax`, `ax` the lower 16 bits and `al` the lowest 8 bits (one byte). `ah` is the byte above `al` (bits 8 to 15). `rbx`, `rcx` and `rdx` have the same parts, for example `ebx`, `bx`, `bl` and `bh`. For `r8` to `r15` the parts are called `r8d`, `r8w` and `r8b`.
registers.lesson.8: Characters are numbers too. In the ASCII table, `'A'` is `65`, `'B'` is `66`, `'0'` is `48` and the newline is `10`. NASM turns a character in single quotes into its number. A number that starts with `0x` is hexadecimal: `0x41` is `65`, and every two hex digits are one byte.
registers.lesson.9: To print a character from a register, copy its byte into memory and write that memory. `mov [char], bl` copies the byte in `bl` to the label `char`. The square brackets mean the memory at that address. The unit about memory explains them in detail.
registers.lesson.11: `0x4F4B` has two bytes: `0x4F` is `'O'` and `0x4B` is `'K'`. The low byte `0x4B` is in `bl`, and the byte above it, `0x4F`, is in `bh`.
registers.lesson.12: Writing to a 32-bit part like `eax` sets the upper 32 bits of `rax` to zero. Writing to `ax`, `al` or `ah` changes only that part and keeps the rest of `rax`.
registers.lesson.13: Both sides of `mov` must have the same size. `mov rax, rbx` and `mov al, bl` work, but `mov al, rbx` is an error.
registers.card.3: writing `eax` clears the upper half of `rax`
registers.card.4: `'A'` is the number `65`, and `0x41` is hex for `65`
registers-1.prompt: What is in `rbx` after this code?
registers-1.explain: `mov rbx, rax` copies the `7`. Changing `rax` later does not change `rbx`.
registers-2.prompt: What is in `rcx` at the end?
registers-2.explain: The last `mov` copies the value of `rdx`, which is `3`, into `rcx`.
registers-3.statement: `mov rax, rbx` copies the value of `rax` into `rbx`.
registers-3.explain: The destination comes first: `mov rax, rbx` copies `rbx` into `rax`.
registers-4.prompt: Match each name with the part of the register.
registers-5.prompt: Complete the code so it prints Hello.
registers-5.explain: `rdx` is the number of bytes to write, and `rbx` holds `5`. `bl` is too small for `rdx`, and `rsi` holds an address.
registers-6.explain: `al` has 8 bits and `rbx` has 64 bits. Both sides of `mov` must have the same size.
registers-7.explain: `0x43` is the byte in `bh`, and `0x43` is `67`, the letter `C`. `bl` holds `0x44`, the letter `D`.
registers-8.prompt: Build the line that copies the value of `rsi` into `rdi`.
registers-8.explain: The destination `rdi` comes first, then the source `rsi`.
registers-9.prompt: What is in `rax` after this code?
registers-9.explain: Writing to `eax` sets the upper 32 bits of `rax` to zero, so only `5` is left.
registers-10.explain: Writing to `al` changes only the lowest byte. The `0x12` above it stays.
registers-11.prompt: These lines should print Hello. Which line has the bug?
registers-11.explain: The destination comes first. To copy `5` from `rcx` into `rdx`, write `mov rdx, rcx`.
registers-12.prompt: Put the lines in order so that `rax` and `rbx` swap their values.
registers-12.explain: First save `rax` in `rcx`, then overwrite `rax` with `rbx`, and finally copy the saved value into `rbx`.
arithmetic.title: Arithmetic
arithmetic.summary: Calculate with add, sub, inc, dec, imul and div, and print the result as a single digit.
arithmetic.lesson.0: `add destination, source` adds the source to the destination and stores the result in the destination. `sub destination, source` subtracts in the same way. Like with `mov`, the source can be an immediate or a register.
arithmetic.lesson.1: To print a number from 0 to 9, turn it into its character. The digits `'0'` to `'9'` are the numbers `48` to `57`, in this order. So you add `'0'` (that is `48`) to the number: `3 + '0'` is `'3'`. This works only for one digit.
arithmetic.lesson.4: `inc` adds 1 to a register and `dec` subtracts 1. They are shorter than `add rbx, 1` and `sub rbx, 1`, and you see them often in loops.
arithmetic.lesson.7: `imul destination, source` multiplies the destination by the source and keeps the result in the destination. The source can be a register or an immediate, for example `imul rbx, 3`.
arithmetic.lesson.10: `div` works differently. It divides the number in `rdx` and `rax` together (`rdx` is the upper half) by the register you give it. The **quotient** goes into `rax` and the **remainder** into `rdx`. So you put the number into `rax`, set `rdx` to `0` and then divide. Here `17 / 5` is `3` with remainder `2`.
arithmetic.lesson.12: The data of `quotient` and `remainder` lies next to each other in memory, 4 bytes in total. That is why one write with `rdx` = `4` prints both lines.
arithmetic.lesson.13: Always set `rdx` to `0` before `div`. Otherwise its old value becomes part of the number, and the result is wrong or the program crashes. Dividing by `0` also crashes the program. `div` needs a register: `div 5` is an error.
arithmetic.card.0: `add rbx, 5` and `sub rbx, rcx` store the result in `rbx`
arithmetic.card.3: `div rcx` divides `rdx:rax` by `rcx`: quotient in `rax`, remainder in `rdx`
arithmetic.card.4: `add bl, '0'` turns 0–9 into its digit character
arithmetic-1.prompt: What is in `rbx` at the end?
arithmetic-2.prompt: What is in `rax` at the end?
arithmetic-3.explain: `23 / 4` is `5` with remainder `3`. The remainder goes into `rdx`.
arithmetic-4.prompt: After `div rcx`, which register holds the quotient?
arithmetic-4.explain: `div` puts the quotient into `rax` and the remainder into `rdx`. `rcx` keeps the divisor.
arithmetic-5.statement: `add rax, rbx` stores the sum in `rbx`.
arithmetic-5.explain: The result always goes into the first operand, the destination. Here that is `rax`.
arithmetic-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 6.
arithmetic-6.explain: Adding `'0'` (48) turns the number `6` into the character `'6'` (54).
arithmetic-7.prompt: Build the line that multiplies `rbx` by `rcx` and keeps the result in `rbx`.
arithmetic-7.explain: `imul` stores the product in its first operand, so `rbx` comes first.
arithmetic-8.prompt: These lines should put the digit of `20 / 4` into `digit`. Which line has the bug?
arithmetic-8.explain: `div rax` divides by `20` itself. The divisor `4` is in `rcx`, so write `div rcx`.
arithmetic-9.prompt: Match the instruction with what it does.
arithmetic-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so that `rbx` ends up with 20.
arithmetic-10.explain: First `rbx` gets `2`, then `2 + 3` is `5`, and `5 * 4` is `20`.
arithmetic-11.explain: `3 * 3` is `9`, and adding `'0'` turns it into the character `9`.
arithmetic-12.explain: `7 / 2` is `3` with remainder `1`. The code prints the remainder from `dl`.
jumps.title: Comparisons and jumps
jumps.summary: Compare values with cmp and use jumps to build if and else in assembly.
jumps.lesson.0: The CPU runs instructions one after another. A **jump** makes it continue at a label instead. `jmp label` always jumps.
jumps.lesson.2: `jmp print` skips `mov rsi, two`, so `rsi` still holds the address of `one`. A label like `print:` can mark any place in the code.
jumps.lesson.4: `cmp a, b` compares two values. It calculates `a - b`, but it does not store the result. Instead it sets **flags**: single bits in the CPU that describe the result. For example, the zero flag is set when the result is `0`, that is, when `a` and `b` are equal.
jumps.lesson.5: A **conditional jump** reads the flags. It jumps only if its condition is true; otherwise the CPU continues with the next line. After `cmp a, b`, `je` jumps if `a` is equal to `b`, `jne` if they are not equal, `jl` if `a` is less than `b` and `jg` if it is greater. `jle` means less or equal, `jge` greater or equal.
jumps.lesson.8: If `rbx` is greater than `5`, the program jumps to `is_big`. Otherwise it runs the lines after `jg` (the else part) and then jumps over the if part with `jmp print`. Both ways meet again at `print`.
jumps.lesson.10: For an if without else, jump over the code when the condition is false. So you use the opposite condition. This code keeps the bigger of two numbers in `rax`: it copies `rbx` into `rax` only when `rax` is less than `rbx`, so it skips the copy with `jge`.
jumps.lesson.12: `je` and `jz` (jump if zero) are the same instruction, and so are `jne` and `jnz`. `add`, `sub`, `inc` and `dec` also set the flags, so a conditional jump can follow them directly.
jumps.lesson.13: The first operand of `cmp` cannot be an immediate. `cmp 5, rax` is an error; write `cmp rax, 5` and choose the jump for that order.
jumps.card.0: `cmp a, b` compares and sets the flags
jumps.card.2: `je`, `jne`, `jl`, `jg`, `jle`, `jge` jump only if the condition is true
jumps.card.3: if: `cmp`, then jump over the code with the opposite condition
jumps-1.statement: `cmp rax, rbx` stores the difference `rax - rbx` in `rax`.
jumps-1.explain: `cmp` only sets the flags. Both registers keep their values.
jumps-2.prompt: What is in `rbx` at the end?
jumps-2.explain: `rax` is equal to `5`, so `je` jumps to `equal`, and `rbx` gets `2`.
jumps-3.explain: `3` is not greater than `7`, so `jg` does not jump. The else part chooses `small` and then jumps to `print`.
jumps-4.prompt: Complete the code so it jumps to `less` only when `rax` is less than 10.
jumps-4.explain: `jl` jumps if `rax` is less than `10`. `jle` would also jump when `rax` is `10`.
jumps-5.prompt: Build the line that compares `rcx` with 0.
jumps-5.explain: `cmp` takes the register first and the immediate second. `cmp 0, rcx` is an error.
jumps-6.prompt: Match the jump with its condition.
jumps-7.prompt: These lines should keep the bigger number in `rax`. Which line has the bug?
jumps-7.explain: The copy must be skipped when `rax` is already the bigger number. Write `jge done`.
jumps-8.prompt: Put the lines in order: if `rax` is less than 5, add 10 to it; otherwise subtract 1.
jumps-8.explain: First compare. If `rax` is not less than `5`, jump to `other` and subtract 1. Otherwise add 10 and jump over the else part.
jumps-9.prompt: After `cmp rax, rbx`, which jump jumps only when `rax` is greater than or equal to `rbx`?
jumps-9.explain: `jge` means jump if greater or equal. `jg` does not jump when the values are equal.
jumps-10.explain: `6` is not less than `4`, so `jl` does not jump, and `sub` makes `rax` `2`.
jumps-11.explain: `1` is not greater than `2`, so `jg` does not jump, and the CPU continues with the next line.
jumps-12.prompt: These lines should print small. Which line has the bug?
jumps-12.explain: After the else part, the code must jump over the if part. Write `jmp print`.
loops.title: Loops
loops.summary: Repeat code with a counter and a jump back, and write loops that print digits and letters.
loops.lesson.0: A loop is a jump backwards. You put a label at the top of the code you want to repeat. At the end, a conditional jump goes back to the label as long as there is work left.
loops.lesson.2: `rbx` is the **counter**. It starts at `3`, and `dec rbx` subtracts 1 after every print. `dec` also sets the zero flag, and `jnz again` (jump if not zero) jumps back while `rbx` is not `0`. After the third print, `rbx` is `0` and the loop ends.
loops.lesson.3: `syscall` changes `rcx` and `r11` (and puts its result into `rax`). So a loop that makes system calls must not keep its counter in `rcx`. Use `rbx` or `r12` to `r15`: system calls keep their values.
loops.lesson.5: A counter can also count up. Here `rbx` goes from `0` to `4`. Each round copies the counter into `al`, turns it into a digit and prints it. `cmp rbx, 5` and `jl next` repeat the loop while `rbx` is less than `5`.
loops.lesson.8: Sometimes the loop must check its condition before the first round, like a `while` loop in Python. Then the check comes at the top, and a `jmp` at the end goes back to it. This loop adds `1 + 2 + 3`. It makes no system calls, so `rcx` is fine as a counter.
loops.lesson.11: Letters follow each other in the ASCII table, so `inc` turns `'A'` into `'B'`. This loop prints the letters from `A` to `E` and then a newline. It stops when `bl` reaches `'F'`.
loops.lesson.13: Make sure that the loop condition becomes false at some point. If the counter never reaches its end value, the loop never stops.
loops.card.0: loop: a label at the top and a conditional jump back
loops.card.1: `dec rbx` and `jnz top` repeat until `rbx` is 0
loops.card.2: `inc rbx`, `cmp rbx, 5` and `jl top` count up to 5
loops.card.3: `syscall` changes `rax`, `rcx` and `r11`: keep counters in `rbx` or `r12`
loops-1.prompt: What is in `rax` at the end?
loops-1.explain: The loop runs 4 times, because `rcx` goes from `4` down to `0`. Each round adds `2`, so `rax` is `8`.
loops-2.explain: The loop prints `a`, `b` and `c`. When `bl` becomes `'d'`, `jne` does not jump, so `d` is not printed.
loops-3.explain: `syscall` overwrites `rcx` and `r11`. That is why a loop with system calls keeps its counter in `rbx` or `r12` to `r15`.
loops-4.prompt: Complete the code so it prints three stars.
loops-4.explain: The counter starts at `3`, and `dec` with `jnz` repeats the print until it reaches `0`: 3 rounds.
loops-5.prompt: Complete the code so the loop repeats until `rbx` is 0.
loops-5.explain: `jnz` jumps back while the result of `dec` is not zero. `jz` and `je` would jump only when it is zero.
loops-6.prompt: Build the line that compares the character in `bl` with the letter Z.
loops-6.explain: A character goes in single quotes. Without them, NASM looks for a label called `Z`.
loops-7.prompt: `rax` starts at 0. Put the lines in order so that `rax` ends up with 15.
loops-7.explain: The counter is set once before the label. Inside the loop, `add` comes before `dec`, so that `jnz` checks the flags of `dec`.
loops-8.prompt: These lines should print the digits 0 to 4. Which line has the bug?
loops-8.explain: The loop must go back while `bl` is less than `'5'`. With `jg` it stops after the first digit. Write `jl next`.
loops-9.prompt: Match the code with its role in a loop.
loops-9.pairs.0: marks the start of the loop
loops-9.pairs.1: counts down and sets the flags
loops-9.pairs.2: jumps back while the result is not zero
loops-10.prompt: A loop makes a system call in every round. Which register is a safe counter?
loops-11.prompt: How many times does this code print Hi?
loops-11.explain: `rbx` takes the values `0`, `2` and `4` when the loop prints. After the third round it is `6`, which is not less than `6`.
loops-12.prompt: What is in `rbx` after this loop?
loops-12.explain: The loop adds `4`, `3`, `2` and `1` before `rcx` reaches `0`: `4 + 3 + 2 + 1` is `10`.
memory.title: Memory and data
memory.summary: Define data in section .data and .bss, read and change memory with [address] and give the size with byte or qword.
memory.lesson.0: Memory is a long row of bytes. Every byte has a number, its **address**. A label is a name for an address. `mov rsi, msg` puts the address of `msg` into `rsi`. With square brackets you get what is stored there: `mov al, [msg]` copies the first byte of `msg` into `al`.
memory.lesson.1: In `section .data` you define data with a start value. `db` defines bytes (1 byte each), `dw` words (2 bytes), `dd` double words (4 bytes) and `dq` quad words (8 bytes). For example, `count dq 5` reserves 8 bytes that hold the number `5`.
memory.lesson.3: `[name+2]` is the byte 2 places after `name`, so the third letter. The offset can also be a register: `[numbers+rbx]` uses the value of `rbx`, which is perfect for loops. For `dq` data, each item has 8 bytes, so the item after `values` is at `[values+8]`.
memory.lesson.6: To store an immediate in memory, you must tell NASM the size, because no register shows it. The size words are `byte` (1 byte), `word` (2), `dword` (4) and `qword` (8). `mov byte [name], 'B'` changes only the first letter.
memory.lesson.8: Numbers in memory work the same way. `add qword [count], 4` adds `4` to the 8 bytes at `count`. `mov rax, [count]` reads 8 bytes, because `rax` has 8 bytes, so no size word is needed there.
memory.lesson.11: `section .bss` reserves memory without a start value; Linux fills it with zeros. `resb 3` reserves 3 bytes, and `resw`, `resd` and `resq` reserve words, double words and quad words. In `section .data`, `len equ $ - msg` calculates a length for you: `$` is the current address, so `$ - msg` is the number of bytes since `msg`. `equ` gives a name to a number; it does not use memory.
memory.lesson.13: Always give the size when you store an immediate in memory, as in `mov qword [count], 5`. Without it, NASM reports an error or guesses the size, depending on its version. One instruction also cannot copy from memory to memory: `mov [a], [b]` is an error, so go through a register.
memory.card.1: `mov rsi, msg` gives the address, `mov al, [msg]` the byte there
memory.card.2: `[msg+2]` and `[numbers+rbx]` add an offset to the address
memory.card.3: `mov byte [x], 'A'` and `add qword [n], 1` name the size
memory-1.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
memory-2.explain: `[name+2]` is the third byte of `Rust`, which is `s`. The first byte is at `name+0`.
memory-3.prompt: What does `mov rsi, msg` put into `rsi`?
memory-3.options.1: the first byte of the text
memory-3.explain: A label is an address. Without square brackets you get the address itself, not the bytes stored there.
memory-4.statement: This code copies the value of `b` into `a`.
memory-4.explain: One instruction cannot read and write memory at the same time, so NASM reports an error. Copy through a register: `mov rax, [b]` and then `mov [a], rax`.
memory-5.prompt: Complete the code so it prints Cat.
memory-5.explain: Only one letter changes, so the size is `byte`. A larger size would also overwrite the next letters with zeros.
memory-6.prompt: What is in `rax` after this code?
memory-6.explain: Each `dq` item has 8 bytes. `[numbers+8]` skips the first item, so `rax` gets the second one.
memory-7.prompt: What is in `rbx` at the end?
memory-7.explain: `add qword [count], 3` changes the value in memory from `5` to `8`, and `mov` reads it into `rbx`.
memory-8.prompt: Build the line that copies the byte at `text+1` into `al`.
memory-8.explain: The square brackets read the memory at the address. Without them, you would get the address itself.
memory-9.prompt: These lines should add the three numbers in `numbers` into `al`. Which line has the bug?
memory-9.explain: `[numbers]` is always the first number. Use the counter as the offset: `add al, [numbers+rbx]`.
memory-10.prompt: `count` holds 2. Put the lines in order so that `count` holds 7 at the end.
memory-10.explain: Read the value into a register, calculate `2 * 3 + 1`, and store the result back into memory.
memory-11.prompt: Which line reserves memory for 4 quad words in `section .bss`?
memory-11.explain: `resq 4` reserves 4 items of 8 bytes. `dq 4` defines one quad word with the value `4`, and `resb 4` reserves only 4 bytes.
memory-12.prompt: What is in `rbx` at the end?
memory-12.explain: `$ - msg` counts the bytes from `msg` to this place: 5 letters and the newline.
stack.title: The stack
stack.summary: Save values on the stack with push and pop, and jump to code and back with call and ret.
stack.lesson.0: The **stack** is an area of memory for temporary values. The register `rsp` (stack pointer) holds the address of the value on top. `push rax` puts the value of `rax` on top: it subtracts 8 from `rsp` and stores the 8 bytes there. `pop rbx` copies the top value into `rbx` and adds 8 to `rsp`.
stack.lesson.2: The value you push last comes back first. This rule is called **last in, first out**. `'B'` was pushed after `'A'`, so the first `pop` gets `'B'`.
stack.lesson.4: `rbx` keeps the old value of `rsp`. After `push`, `rsp` is 8 smaller, so the difference is `8`: the stack grows down, toward smaller addresses. `pop` adds the 8 again.
stack.lesson.6: With `push` and `pop` you can keep a value safe while a register is busy. Remember that `syscall` changes `rcx`. This loop still counts with `rcx`: it pushes the counter before the system call and pops it back afterwards.
stack.lesson.9: A **function** is a piece of code that you can run from several places. `call print_hi` pushes the **return address** (the address of the instruction after `call`) and jumps to `print_hi`. At the end of the function, `ret` pops this address and jumps back to it.
stack.lesson.11: Put your functions after the exit call. Then the CPU reaches them only through `call`, and never by running into them from the code above.
stack.lesson.12: Every `push` in a function needs its `pop` before `ret`. Otherwise `ret` takes the wrong value from the stack as its return address, and the program crashes.
stack.lesson.13: `[rsp]` is the value on top of the stack. `mov rax, [rsp]` reads it without removing it.
stack.card.1: `pop rax` takes the top value back (`rsp` + 8)
stack.card.3: `call f` pushes the return address and jumps to `f`; `ret` jumps back
stack-1.prompt: What is in `rbx` at the end?
stack-1.explain: The first `pop` gets `3`, the last value pushed. The second `pop` gets `2`.
stack-2.prompt: How many bytes smaller is `rsp` after this code?
stack-2.explain: Three `push` instructions subtract `24`, and one `pop` adds `8` back.
stack-3.statement: The stack grows toward higher addresses.
stack-3.explain: `push` subtracts 8 from `rsp`, so the stack grows toward smaller addresses.
stack-4.prompt: Complete the code so that `rax` and `rbx` swap their values.
stack-4.explain: The old `rbx` was pushed last, so `pop rax` gets it. The old `rax` is still on the stack, and `pop rbx` gets it.
stack-5.prompt: Put the lines in order: the function `f` returns 5 in `rax` and gives `rbx` back unchanged.
stack-5.explain: The label comes first. Save `rbx`, use it, copy the result into `rax`, restore `rbx` and return.
stack-6.prompt: Build the line that reads the top value of the stack into `rax` without removing it.
stack-6.explain: `[rsp]` is the memory at the address in `rsp`, which is the top value. `mov rax, rsp` would copy the address itself.
stack-7.prompt: The function should add 2 to `rax` and give `rbx` back unchanged. Which line has the bug?
stack-7.explain: The saved value belongs to `rbx`. `pop rax` overwrites the result. Write `pop rbx`.
stack-8.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
stack-8.pairs.0: puts a value on the stack
stack-8.pairs.1: takes the top value from the stack
stack-8.pairs.2: saves the return address and jumps
stack-8.pairs.3: jumps back to the return address
stack-8.pairs.4: holds the address of the top value
stack-9.prompt: What does `call` push on the stack?
stack-9.options.0: the address of the instruction after `call`
stack-9.explain: `call` pushes the return address. `ret` later pops it and jumps back there.
stack-10.explain: The first `pop` gets `'C'`, the second gets `'B'`. Only the second value is printed.
stack-11.explain: Each `call` runs `add_one` once, and `ret` comes back to the next line. `rbx` goes from `0` to `3`.
stack-12.statement: This program prints Hi exactly once.
stack-12.explain: There is no exit call, so after `call` returns, the CPU runs into `print_hi` again and prints a second Hi. Then `ret` finds no return address, and the program crashes.
functions.title: Functions
functions.summary: Pass arguments in rdi and rsi, return results in rax, save registers and write a small print function.
functions.lesson.0: Functions work together because they follow the same rules, the **calling convention**. On Linux, the first arguments go into `rdi`, `rsi`, `rdx`, `rcx`, `r8` and `r9`, in this order. The function puts its result into `rax`.
functions.lesson.2: `_start` passes `2` in `rdi` and `5` in `rsi`. `add_numbers` copies the first argument into `rax`, adds the second one and returns. After the `call`, the result is in `rax`.
functions.lesson.4: A function may change `rax`, `rcx`, `rdx`, `rsi`, `rdi` and `r8` to `r11`. If you still need their values after a call, save them before. But a function must give back `rbx`, `rbp` and `r12` to `r15` unchanged. If it uses them, it pushes them at the start and pops them, in reverse order, before `ret`.
functions.lesson.6: The loop keeps its counter in `rbx`. `print_digit` changes `rax`, `rdi`, `rsi` and `rdx`, and its system call changes `rcx` and `r11`. None of them is `rbx`, so the counter is safe.
functions.lesson.8: `square` needs a register for its work and uses `rbx`. So it pushes `rbx` first and pops it before `ret`. That is why `rbx` is still `2` in `_start` after the call.
functions.lesson.10: This function `print` gets the address of a text in `rdi` and its length in `rsi`. The write system call needs them in `rsi` and `rdx`. So `print` first copies `rsi` into `rdx` and then `rdi` into `rsi`. The other order would overwrite `rsi` before it is copied.
functions.lesson.12: After a `call`, do not expect `rax`, `rcx`, `rdx`, `rsi`, `rdi` or `r8` to `r11` to have their old values. Keep values that you need later in `rbx` or `r12` to `r15`, or push them before the call.
functions.lesson.13: Every function ends with `ret`, and every `push` inside it needs a `pop`. Keep functions short: one function, one job.
functions.card.3: it must keep `rbx`, `rbp`, `r12`–`r15`: save them with `push` and `pop`
functions-1.prompt: Which register holds the first argument of a function?
functions-1.explain: The arguments go into `rdi`, `rsi`, `rdx`, `rcx`, `r8` and `r9`. `rsi` holds the second one.
functions-2.prompt: Where does a function put its result?
functions-2.explain: By the calling convention, the result goes into `rax`.
functions-3.prompt: What is in `rax` when `call triple` returns?
functions-3.explain: `triple` copies the argument `4` from `rdi` into `rax` and multiplies it by `3`.
functions-4.statement: A function may change `rbx` and leave it changed when it returns.
functions-4.explain: `rbx`, `rbp` and `r12` to `r15` must have their old values after the call. A function that uses `rbx` saves it with `push` and restores it with `pop`.
functions-5.prompt: Complete the function so it returns the first argument minus the second.
functions-5.explain: The first argument is in `rdi`. The function copies it into `rax` and subtracts the second argument `rsi`.
functions-6.prompt: `print` expects the address in `rdi` and the length in `rsi`. These lines should print Hi. Which line has the bug?
functions-6.explain: The second argument goes into `rsi`, not `rdx`. Write `mov rsi, 3`.
functions-7.prompt: Put the lines in order: `square` returns `rdi * rdi` in `rax` and keeps `rbx`.
functions-7.explain: Save `rbx` first, copy the argument, multiply, put the result into `rax`, restore `rbx` and return.
functions-8.prompt: Build the line that passes 7 as the first argument.
functions-9.prompt: Match the register with its role in the calling convention.
functions-9.pairs.4: must be kept by the function
functions-10.prompt: What does this program print? Write the digits in order.
functions-10.explain: The loop calls `print_digit` with `3`, `2` and `1`. `rbx` keeps the counter, because `print_digit` does not change it.
functions-11.prompt: What is in `r12` when `call double` returns?
functions-11.explain: `double` uses `r12`, but it pushes it first and pops it before `ret`, so `r12` is `4` again. The result `6` is in `rax`.
functions-12.explain: `set_two` changes `rbx` and does not restore it, so the program prints `2`. A correct function would push and pop `rbx`.
